title: Designing Medicines
objective: After this level you can explain how chemists design new medicines.
summary: Aspirin grew from willow bark: chemists isolated salicin, made gentler acetylsalicylic acid, and later learned how it works. Today drugs can be designed to fit an enzyme, then tested in phases.

cards.headline: More than 2,000 years ago, people used willow bark as medicine.
cards.body: Chinese and Greek healers both did. Today its descendant comes in a tablet. The road between the two shows how chemists design medicines.

cards.headline: Find it, then fix it
cards.body: In 1828, Johann Büchner pulled the active substance out of willow and named it salicin. Salicylic acid, made from it, eased pain but often irritated the stomach. At the Bayer company, Arthur Eichengrün set chemist Felix Hoffmann the task of making a better version, and in 1897 Hoffmann made acetylsalicylic acid, gentler on the stomach. That's aspirin: nature's molecule, tweaked by chemists.

cards.headline: Then, finally, understand it
cards.body: Here's the humbling part: aspirin was sold for decades before anyone knew how it worked. In 1971, John Vane showed that it blocks the body's making of prostaglandins, substances involved in pain, fever and inflammation. The work shared the 1982 Nobel Prize.

cards.headline: Designing to fit
cards.body: Modern chemists can start from the target instead. For HIV, knowing the crystal structure of a key HIV enzyme, its protease, was critical: chemists designed molecules to fit into it and jam it. The first of these drugs entered clinical use in 1995, one of the great success stories of structure-based drug design.

cards.headline: Then test, carefully
cards.body: A promising molecule then faces people in phases. Phase 1, with 20 to 100 volunteers, studies safety and dosage. Phases 2 and 3, with up to several hundred and then 300 to 3,000 people, test whether it works and watch for side effects.

cards.headline: Medicines: designed
learned: Aspirin began as willow bark; chemists isolated salicin
Acetylsalicylic acid (1897) was gentler on the stomach
Drugs can be designed to fit an enzyme, like HIV protease
New drugs are tested in phases, starting with safety and dosage
